title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 363
paragraphs: Moreover, they resolved to join together and leave a common memorial of themselves. Having decided this, they had a labyrinth built, situated a little above the Lake of Moiris and almost opposite the so-called City of Crocodiles. I saw this myself, and I found it greater than words can describe. For if one should put together and reckon up all the buildings and great works produced by the Greeks, they would prove inferior in labor and expense to this labyrinth — though it is true that both the temple at Ephesos and the one at Samos are works worth noting. The pyramids too were greater than words can say, and each one of them is equal to many Greek works, great as those may be; but the labyrinth surpasses even the pyramids. It has twelve roofed courts, with gates facing each other, six on the north side and six on the south, adjoining one another, and the same wall surrounds them all on the outside. It contains two kinds of chambers, one kind below ground and the other above them — three thousand in number, fifteen hundred of each kind. The upper chambers we saw ourselves, going through them, and we speak of them having looked with our own eyes. But the underground chambers we only heard about, for the Egyptians in charge of them refused to show them on any account, saying that there lay the tombs of the kings who had first built this labyrinth and of the sacred crocodiles. So we speak of the chambers below from what we received by hearsay, while the chambers above we saw ourselves and found to be works of more than human greatness. The passages through the chambers and the windings through the courts, which were beautifully adorned, offered endless matter for wonder, as we went from a court into the chambers beyond, from the chambers into colonnades, from the colonnades into other rooms, and then from the chambers again into other courts. Over all of these is a roof made of stone like the walls, and the walls are covered with carved figures; each court is surrounded by pillars of white stone fitted together most perfectly. At the end of the labyrinth, at one corner, there is a pyramid forty fathoms high, on which large figures are carved, and an underground passage leads to it.
